The independent protective effect of female gender on multiple organ failure and nosocomial infection rates remains significant in both premenopausal and postmenopausal women when compared with similarly aged men.

The available research suggests that hormonal differences may not be the primary reason for these gender-based differences after injury and hemorrhagic shock. Previous studies have shown that physiologic sex hormone changes that occur after menopause in women may not play a significant role in these outcomes. This implies that factors other than sex hormones are responsible for the observed differences.

In summary, the evidence suggests that female gender is still an important factor in predicting multiple organ failure and nosocomial infection rates after injury and hemorrhagic shock, regardless of premenopausal or postmenopausal status.
